# Deleting one nonvertex fiber: exact realization, compensation, and a depth dip

The maximum **normalized** mixed halfspace depth need not be monotone or
quasiconcave while one nonvertex fiber contracts to the fiber forced by all
remaining sources. This occurs already for three positive interval fibers.
The construction below changes exactly that one actual fiber. It is distinct
from a common Minkowski addend or a translation shadow system.

## 1. The exact one-fiber contraction

Let `P` be a finite integer set and let compact convex fibers `K_p` be
induced by their hull

    C=conv union_(p in P) ({p} x K_p),

with no additional nonempty integer fibers. Fix a nonvertex `z` of `conv P`
and assume all `K_p` are full dimensional in the continuous space. Set

    C^-=conv union_(p!=z) ({p} x K_p),   B=(C^-)_z.

The projection remains `conv P`, so `B` is nonempty; a representation of
`z` using the other bases and their full-dimensional fibers shows that `B`
is full dimensional. Also `B subset K_z`. Every other fiber is unchanged:
`C^- subset C`, while the entire original `K_p` remains a generating fiber
for each `p!=z`.

For `0<=t<=1`, put

    K_z(t)=(1-t)B+t K_z,
    C_t=conv(({z} x K_z(t)) union
             union_(p!=z)({p} x K_p)).                 (1)

Then the ACTUAL fiber of `C_t` at `z` is exactly `K_z(t)`, all other fibers
are `K_p`, and there are no new integer indices. Indeed `C_t subset C` and
retains all the other fibers. A convex combination at base `z` either uses
only its own generating fiber or, after removing its own coefficient,
has remaining continuous coordinate in `B`. Since `B subset K_z(t)`, the
whole combination lies in `K_z(t)`. This proves equality at the target.
The unchanged projection proves the last assertion. The bodies in (1)
are nested as `t` increases, because `B subset K_z`.

This also clarifies the word "deletion": the target's generating set is
removed, but its nonempty forced fiber `B` remains. No other retained fiber
is silently replaced or contracted.

## 2. A universal mass correction

For a nonempty induced source of positive mixed d-volume, write

    M_C=mu_C(S_C),
    A_C=max_(y in S_C) inf_(H closed, y in H) mu_C(H),
    beta_C=A_C/M_C.

If `D subset C` are convex bodies and `M_D>0`, and if
`delta=M_C-M_D`, then

    0 <= A_C-A_D <= delta.                            (2)

To prove this without assuming that the original maximizing point survives,
extend the unnormalized depth function to every point of
`Lambda=Z^n x R^d`. Since `mu_D<=mu_C` and their difference has mass `delta`,
these depth functions satisfy pointwise

    A_mu_D(y) <= A_mu_C(y) <= A_mu_D(y)+delta.

Every point outside `D` has zero `mu_D` depth by strict separation from the
compact convex set `D`. Consequently the supremum over all of `Lambda`
is the same as the maximum over `S_D`; the analogous statement holds for
`C`. Taking suprema proves (2). In particular a removed maximizing point
cannot cause a further unaccounted loss.

The normalized bounds are therefore

 max(0,(M_C beta_C-delta)/(M_C-delta)) <= beta_D
       <= min(1,M_C beta_C/(M_C-delta)),               (3)

and in the other direction

 (M_D/M_C) beta_D <= beta_C
       <= (M_D beta_D+delta)/M_C.                     (4)

These are compensation bounds, not monotonicity of normalized depth. They
apply to (1), where the mass loss is exactly the lost volume of its single
target fiber. No coefficient smaller than one is asserted in (2).

## 3. Exact counterexample throughout the contraction

Take `n=d=1`, `P={-1,0,1}`, and, for `b>=1`,

    K_-1=K_1=[0,1],    K_0=[0,b].

The actual convex body is

    C_b={(z,x): -1<=z<=1, 0<=x<=b-(b-1)|z|}.

Deleting the nonvertex middle generator leaves the rectangle
`[-1,1] x [0,1]`, so the forced middle fiber is `[0,1]`.
Starting from `b=5`, the contraction (1) is exactly `b=1+4t`.
All bodies and all three fibers have positive dimension for every
`0<=t<=1`, and total mixed mass is `M_b=b+2`.

Here is the complete all-halfspace depth computation. Let
`c(s)=max(0,min(1,s))`. A downward cap through `(0,x)`, `0<=x<=b`, has mass

    x+c(x+v)+c(x-v).

For every `x>=0`,

    min_v [c(x+v)+c(x-v)] = min(2x,1).                (5)

For `x<=1/2`, the unclipped pair gives `2x`; clipping either member
cannot lower the sum below `2x`. For `x>=1/2`, either both are interior
and sum to `2x>=1`, or one is at least one; if one is nonpositive the
other is at least `2x>=1`. A sufficiently large finite slope attains
sum one. Thus (5) holds, with an attained finite slope in every case.
Reflection within each endpoint interval yields the upward infimum

    L(x)=x+min(2x,1),
    U(x)=b-x+min(2(1-x)_+,1).                        (6)

The vertical caps through the middle fiber have mass `b+1`, no less than
the values in (6). Any containing cap can first be translated through the
point without increasing its mass. Thus the exact absolute depth there is
`min(L(x),U(x))`, including all oblique and vertical closed halfspaces.

The first function in (6) is strictly increasing and the second strictly
decreasing. For `1<=b<=3`, their intersection is
`x=(b+1)/4`, in `[1/2,1]`, and the absolute depth is `(b+5)/4`.
For `b>=3`, their intersection is `x=(b-1)/2>=1`, and the absolute depth
is `(b+1)/2`. At an endpoint integer base, large finite tilts isolate either
own-fiber half-interval; its largest depth is exactly `1/2`, smaller than
the middle maximum. Therefore the global normalized maximum is exactly

    beta(b)=(b+5)/(4(b+2)),  1<=b<=3;
            (b+1)/(2(b+2)),  b>=3.                  (7)

Consequently along (1),

    beta(C_0)=1/2,
    beta(C_(1/2))=2/5,
    beta(C_1)=3/7.                                  (8)

The middle value is strictly below BOTH endpoint values. In fact the first
branch of (7) decreases strictly in `b`, and the second increases strictly.
This disproves either direction of normalized-depth monotonicity and also
quasiconcavity for this precise nonvertex-fiber deletion interpolation.

For comparison, the absolute maximum along the same deformation is

    A(C_t)=3/2+t,    0<=t<=1/2;
           1+2t,    1/2<=t<=1,

while `M(C_t)=3+4t`. The absolute depth increases, as (2) requires; the
normalization by retained total mass creates the strict dip. The endpoint
absolute loss under complete deletion is `3-3/2=3/2`, with removed mass
`7-3=4`. Thus the exact counterexample does not contradict (2)--(4).

This is a deformation obstruction, not a counterexample to OC: every
maximum in (7) is at least `2/5`, larger than the `n=d=1` target `1/4`.
